title: B.C. woman fatally shot by police in New Brunswick
subtitle: Family members in Tofino have identified the woman as Chantel Moore, a mother of a five-year-old girl
article: A 26-year-old B.C. woman is dead after she was shot by police in New Brunswick early Thursday morning.
Family members in Tofino have identified the woman as Chantel Moore, an Indigenous woman and mother of a five-year-old girl who had just moved to New Brunswick from Port Alberni a few months ago.
A GoFundMe web page has been set up to help Moore's family.
Police in Edmundston, N.B., say at around 2:30 a.m., officers received a request to check on Moore's wellbeing at an apartment building on Canada Road in Edmundston.
Police say she was holding a knife and threatened the officers.

"At first, the officer went on scene, and all of a sudden the person just exited the apartment with a knife and was attacking the officer," Edmundston Police Force Insp. Steve Robinson told CBC News on Thursday. "He had no choice but to defend himself."
Moore died at the apartment, according to police.

"I don't believe this. They were going there to check on her, not kill her," Grace Frank, Moore's grandmother, said in a Facebook post. "Self-defence is what (the police officer) says and she is not here to defend herself. I don't believe."
Nora Martin, Moore's aunt, described her great-niece as a "kind, gentle and loving" person, and had trouble believing she would charge at an officer with a knife.

"It's very out of character. Chantel didn't have a mean bone in her body," said Martin, who works as a community health liaison with the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation. "As far as I'm aware, she never had any trouble with the law."
Moore, who recently started working at a hotel, had just moved into her own place after spending a weeks at her mother's home in Edmundston.
Martin says Moore's boyfriend, who was in Toronto, had asked police to check in on her because she complained to him that she was being harassed by someone.
"He was worried about her," she said. "(The officer) shot her five times. I don't know if it was one bullet that hit her or all of them."
Robinson told reporters that Edmundston police officers do not wear body cameras.
An autopsy has been scheduled, and an investigation is continuing.
Martin says six members of her family are hoping to fly to New Brunswick on Friday to be with Moore's mother and daughter.
The Edmundston police department said he has asked for an independent review of the incident, and New Brunswick RCMP will help with the investigation as "a matter of accountability."
Moore's death comes amid protests against police violence in Canada and the U.S.
"I hope there is a full investigation," said Martin.
The EIB, Quebec's independent police watchdog, said late Thursday that it will be investigating the shooting at the request of RCMP.
On Thursday, Lydia Hwitsum, a spokesperson for the First Nations Summit Political Executive, called for a full, independent and impartial investigation into Moore's death as soon as possible.

"Her family deserves answers to the circumstances that led to her tragic death at the hands of the Edmundston Police Department. Indigenous people in Canada face clear systemic racial bias by police forces. This systemic racism must stop. Indigenous lives matter. The lives of Indigenous women and girls matters," said Hwitsum.

One-third of the people shot to death by RCMP officers over a 10-year period were First Nations, despite Indigenous people only making up five per cent of the population, according to information obtained by the Globe and Mail in 2019.

Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, president of the B.C. Union of Indian Chiefs, said he was outraged that amidst global action decrying police brutality, a wellness check for an Indigenous woman has resulted in her death at the hands of police.

"This sickening pattern of death after death, of Chantel Moore's name being added to the ever-growing list of lives stolen by racism, it must be stopped and I believe an inevitable reckoning has arrived," said Phillip in an email to Postmedia.

"I grieve with Chantel's family, and I know she will not be forgotten, as the whole world is watching the ramifications of generations of racialized oppression and police brutality and we are demanding change."
